DuckDB npm Account Compromise

Target: duckdb · repo
Date: 2025-09-09
Actor: Third Party (group)
Target Kind: library
Language: JavaScript
Cause: social_engineering
Motive: financial_gain
Transitive: false
Impact: financial_exploitation
User Impact: 5
Phase: distribution
Campaigns: Qix npm Phishing Package Compromise

Synopsis

The duckdb_admin npm account was compromised via a phishing email linking to a cloned npmjs site, allowing attackers to bypass 2FA and inject a new API token. The attackers published malicious DuckDB npm packages carrying the same wallet-drainer family used in the Qix/debug/chalk compromise. JFrog later named duckdb, @duckdb/node-bindings, @duckdb/duckdb-wasm, and @duckdb/node-api as follow-on packages in the ongoing September 2025 npm phishing campaign.

Story

DuckDB was not part of the first public Qix maintainer blast, but it followed the same path through npm trust. The attacker phished npm credentials through a cloned npm login flow, gained publish access, and pushed malicious package versions from the duckdb_admin account.

JFrog's follow-on reporting tied the DuckDB packages to the same ongoing September 2025 npm phishing campaign that had already hit debug, chalk, ansi-regex, strip-ansi, and related packages. That linkage matters because earlier uncertainty left DuckDB looking like a nearby but possibly separate account compromise.

The payload family was the browser-facing wallet drainer from the wider campaign. It used JavaScript obfuscation, hooked web3 and XMLHttpRequest behavior, watched transaction data across multiple chains, and rewrote payment destinations to attacker-controlled addresses before signing.

DuckDB remains a separate attack record because its package owner and artifact scope are distinct from the Qix-maintained utility packages. The campaign membership now captures the shared phishing infrastructure, timing, malware behavior, and JFrog's explicit attribution to the same ongoing npm attack.
